title: Putting It All Together
oneLiner: A map of everything in reinforcement learning: the few big choices that separate all the methods, the one equation behind them, and how to set up a new problem well.

what.html:
All the methods in this subject answer the same question (how to learn good decisions when today's choice shapes tomorrow) and differ in a handful of choices: what they learn, where their learning targets come from, whether they use a model of the world, whether they build on their own guesses, and where their data come from. One idea runs through them all: value now = reward now + discounted value next.

Everyday versionLike learning to cook: you can follow a recipe exactly (planning with a model), taste only the finished dish (Monte Carlo), adjust as you go (TD), copy a chef (imitation), or ask diners which of two dishes they prefer (preferences).

why.html:
• A map helps you pick the right tool and explain your choice.
  • Many bugs come from mixing up basic ideas (reward vs value).
  • Setting the problem up well matters more than the algorithm.

how.title: Five questions
how.html: What is learned? Where do targets come from? Is there a model? Does it bootstrap? How is data collected? Answer these and you've placed the method.

how.title: One recursion everywhere
how.html: Value = reward + γ × next value. Dynamic programming uses it with a rulebook, TD with single experiences, DQN with a network, actor–critic to guide a policy, planning with imagined experience.

how.title: Four things not to mix up
how.html: State (the situation), reward (one immediate number), return (the total you actually got afterwards), value (the total you expect on average).

how.title: From bandits to TD
how.html: Bandits: exploration. DP: planning with a model. MC: whole-episode averages. TD: one-step updates. With reward 2, γ = 0.9, V now 1.0 and V next 1.5, the TD error is 2.35, used by both critics and actors.

how.title: Bigger problems, one update form
how.html: Swap tables for functions or networks (DQN adds replay and a target network). For policies: change θ by (how good it was) × (direction that makes the action more likely), where "how good" is a return, an advantage or a TD error.

how.title: Three separate labels
how.html: Model-based or model-free; value-based or policy-based; on-policy or off-policy. DQN: value-based, off-policy. PPO: policy-based, on-policy. MCTS: model-based planning.

how.title: Set up the problem first
how.html: Who are the agents? What do they observe and control? What's the reward, and does it reward the goal? When do episodes end? Where does data come from, is there a model, what limits apply, and how will you judge success beyond the reward?

demo.html: Pick a real-world scenario (a warehouse robot, ad recommendations, heating control, a coding assistant) and see the modelling checklist filled in, including how success should be judged beyond the training reward.

example.html:
One number, two jobs. Reward 2, γ = 0.9, current estimate 1.0, next-state estimate 1.5: TD error = 2 + 1.35 − 1.0 = 2.35. A critic nudges its estimate up (to 1.235 with α = 0.1); an actor makes the action it just took more likely in proportion to 2.35.

Supplementary On the same small maze with the same budget, Dyna-Q (with planning) reached near-shortest paths fastest; SARSA was the most cautious.

misunderstandings: Each RL algorithm is a completely different idea.
Most differ in one or two of five choices.
Value is the expected return; a return is one sample.
takeaways: The Bellman recursion links DP, TD, DQN, actor–critic and planning.
Keep state, reward, return and value distinct.
Model the problem before choosing the method.
thirty: RL methods differ mainly in what they learn, where targets come from, model use, bootstrapping and data generation. The Bellman recursion (value = reward + γ × next value) underlies DP (with a model), TD and Q-learning (samples), DQN (networks), actor–critic and planning. State, reward, return and value must be kept distinct. Bandits isolate exploration; DP plans; MC averages returns; TD bootstraps, with SARSA, Q-learning and Expected SARSA differing only in the next-action term (worked δ = 2.35). Function approximation and DQN scale value learning; policy gradients use Δθ ∝ signal × ∇log π. Model-based/model-free, value/policy-based and on/off-policy are independent axes (DQN: value, off-policy; PPO: policy, on-policy; MCTS: model-based planning). New problems should be formulated (agents, state, actions, reward, horizon, data, model, output, constraints, evaluation) before choosing an algorithm.
